intuition: All candidate sections have the same length k, so the largest sum also has the largest average. Compute the first sum, then slide one position at a time by removing the leaving value and adding the entering value. Keep the largest sum and divide by k at the end.

Maintain the sum of one fixed-width window. Moving its right boundary by one introduces nums[right] and removes nums[right-k]. Updating those two values gives the next exact window sum in constant time. Initialize the running maximum from the first actual window, rather than from zero.

That initialization matters for an array containing only negatives: zero may be larger than every legitimate average, but it is not a candidate. Keep integer sums during the scan and divide by k once at the end. The first window plus each subsequent one-step slide covers every permitted subarray exactly once.
The technique would need different reasoning if lengths varied, because a larger sum would no longer necessarily imply a larger average.

steps: For nums=[1,12,-5,-6,50,3] and k=4, the first four values sum to 2, so total=best=2.
Move right to index 4. Add 50 and remove nums[0]=1, producing total=51.
Update best from 2 to 51. This window is [12,-5,-6,50].
Move right to index 5. Add 3 and remove nums[1]=12, producing total=42, which does not improve best.
All three length-four windows were measured. Return 51/4=12.75.

codeNotes.note: Starting from a real window prevents an all-negative input from incorrectly returning an unattainable zero average.
Adjacent fixed-width windows differ by exactly these entering and leaving elements, so their sum can be updated without rescanning.
The denominator is shared by every candidate; delaying division retains exact integer sums while comparing windows.

keyDecision: Each update subtracts nums[right - k] and adds nums[right], keeping exactly k values.
